title: Required Aircraft Inspections (AV1ATES)

required_knowledge_points.title: AV1ATES — The Seven Required Inspection Categories
required_knowledge_points.why: DPEs consistently ask applicants to recite and explain the AV1ATES acronym. A student who cannot name all seven items — with their respective intervals — fails the very first airworthiness question.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: AV1ATES stands for: (A) Annual Inspection — every 12 calendar months, conducted by an IA-certificated mechanic per 14 CFR 91.409(a). (V) VOR Check — every 30 days for IFR operations only per 14 CFR 91.171; not required for VFR operations. (1) 100-Hour Inspection — required ONLY when the aircraft carries any person for hire or is provided for flight instruction per 14 CFR 91.409(b); performed by any certificated A&P mechanic (no IA required). (A) Altimeter/Pitot-Static System — every 24 calendar months for IFR operations in controlled airspace per 14 CFR 91.411; not required for VFR. (T) Transponder — every 24 calendar months for all operations requiring a transponder per 14 CFR 91.413. (E) ELT — every 12 calendar months for proper installation and battery, plus battery replacement when 50% of useful life expires or 1 cumulative hour of use occurs per 14 CFR 91.207. (S) Static System — see Altimeter check above; sometimes listed separately for the static pressure system.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### (A) Annual Inspection — 14 CFR 91.409(a)
- Required every **12 calendar months** for all civil aircraft
- Must be performed by an **A&P mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization (IA)**

### (V) VOR Check — 14 CFR 91.171
- Required every **30 days** — **IFR operations only**, not required for VFR

### (1) 100-Hour Inspection — 14 CFR 91.409(b)
- Required **only when** aircraft carries persons **for hire** or is **provided for flight instruction**
- Any **certificated A&P mechanic** can perform it (no IA required)
- **Not required** for personal VFR flights regardless of flight hours

### (A) Altimeter / Pitot-Static System — 14 CFR 91.411
- Required every **24 calendar months** — **IFR in controlled airspace only**

### (T) Transponder — 14 CFR 91.413
- Required every **24 calendar months** — all operations requiring a transponder

### (E) ELT — 14 CFR 91.207
- **12-month** inspection for installation and battery condition
- Battery must be replaced when **50% of useful life expires** OR after **1 cumulative hour of use**

### (S) Static System
- Covered under the Altimeter/Pitot-Static check (same 24-month interval)

required_knowledge_points.title: Annual vs. 100-Hour: Who Performs Them and When Are They Required
required_knowledge_points.why: The most common oral exam mistake is applying the 100-hour requirement to personal VFR flights — the 100-hour inspection is triggered ONLY by commercial use. A second common mistake is assuming a regular A&P can perform an Annual inspection (they cannot without an IA).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: The Annual inspection (91.409(a)) must be conducted by an A&P mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization (IA). A standard A&P mechanic without the IA designation may not approve an aircraft for return to service after an Annual. The Annual must be completed within the preceding 12 calendar months — the expiration falls on the last day of the 12th month. There is NO grace period for an overdue Annual inspection. If it expires overnight, the aircraft needs a Special Flight Permit to move. The 100-Hour inspection (91.409(b)) is required when: (1) the aircraft carries any person (other than a crewmember) FOR HIRE, or (2) the aircraft is provided by a flight instructor for dual instruction. A standard A&P mechanic (without IA) may perform and approve the 100-hour. A completed Annual inspection legally stands as a 100-hour inspection (it resets both clocks). An aircraft more than 100 hours past its last inspection is legal for personal VFR flight (no 100-hour required for non-commercial operations).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Annual Inspection (14 CFR 91.409(a))
- Required for **all civil aircraft**, every 12 calendar months
- Must be performed by an **A&P mechanic with an Inspection Authorization (IA)**
- A standard A&P **without IA** cannot approve return to service
- **No grace period** — an overdue Annual means the aircraft cannot legally move without a **Special Flight Permit**

### 100-Hour Inspection (14 CFR 91.409(b))
- Required **only** when the aircraft carries persons **for hire** OR is **provided for flight training**
- Any **certificated A&P** (no IA required) may perform it
- **NOT required** for personal/private flights regardless of time since last inspection

### Key Relationship
- A completed **Annual** fulfills the **100-Hour** requirement and resets both clocks
- An aircraft used commercially that has 500 hours since its last annual is **still legal** for personal non-commercial flight (no 100-hour needed for private use)

required_knowledge_points.title: The 100-Hour Grace Period — The Math That Catches Everyone
required_knowledge_points.why: The 91.409(b) 10-hour grace period is one of the most tested and most frequently miscalculated items on the checkride. Most applicants know the rule exists but cannot correctly perform the penalty subtraction calculation.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: 14 CFR 91.409(b) allows the 100-hour inspection limit to be exceeded by up to 10 hours ONLY while en route to a maintenance facility where the inspection can be performed. The excess hours accumulated while flying to the maintenance facility are NOT a bonus — they must be subtracted from the next 100-hour interval. Formula: Next 100-hour due = Last inspection time + (100 - overage). Example: 100-hour inspection was due at Tach 800.0. Aircraft flew to maintenance, arriving at Tach 806.0 (6 hours over). The inspection was performed at 806.0. The NEXT inspection is due at 806.0 + 94 = 900.0. The 6-hour overage is NOT added back — it is permanently deducted. A Special Flight Permit is NOT required to exercise the 10-hour grace period; the regulation authorizes the flight to reach maintenance. No Special Flight Permit is needed to move within this authorized window.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The 10-Hour Grace Period (14 CFR 91.409(b))
- The 100-hour limit may be **exceeded by up to 10 hours** ONLY when flying to a maintenance facility
- **No Special Flight Permit required** — the regulation explicitly authorizes this movement
- Cannot be used for regular flights — must be **en route to maintenance**

### The Penalty Subtraction — Exam Math
- Grace period hours are **permanently deducted** from the next 100-hour interval
- Formula: **Next inspection due = Last inspection time + (100 − overage)**

### Example Calculation
| | Tach Time |
|---|---|
| 100-Hour was due | 800.0 |
| Aircraft arrived at maintenance | 806.0 |
| Overage | **6 hours** |
| Inspection performed at | 806.0 |
| **Next 100-Hour due** | 806.0 + 94 = **900.0** |

- The 6-hour overage is **not forgiven** — next interval is only **94 hours**, not 100

required_knowledge_points.title: Maintenance Recordkeeping — The 43.9 Entry Requirements
required_knowledge_points.why: An A&P logbook entry that is missing even one element (e.g., the certificate number) is legally insufficient — the aircraft has not been returned to service, making it unairworthy even if the physical work was done correctly.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Every maintenance entry must comply with 14 CFR 43.9. Four required elements for every logbook entry: (1) A description of the work performed (or reference to data acceptable to the Administrator). (2) The date of completion. (3) The name of the person performing the work. (4) The signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate held by the person approving the return to service. An entry missing any of these elements is legally incomplete. The maintenance records must be retained by the registered owner under 14 CFR 91.417. Required retention period: records of the last Annual, 100-hour, or progressive inspections must be retained until the work is repeated or superseded by another inspection. Records of ADs, major repairs, and alterations must be retained and transferred with the aircraft.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Four Required Elements Per Entry (14 CFR 43.9)
- **Description** of the work performed (or reference to acceptable data)
- **Date** of completion
- **Name** of the person who performed the work
- **Signature, certificate number, and type of certificate** of the person approving return to service

> A missing certificate number = incomplete entry = aircraft NOT legally returned to airworthy condition

### Recordkeeping Retention (14 CFR 91.417)
- Owner is responsible for retaining maintenance records
- **Annual / 100-Hour / Progressive inspections:** retain until **superseded by the next inspection**
- **ADs, major repairs, and alterations:** retain **indefinitely** and must **transfer with the aircraft** upon sale

lesson_overview:
## Required Aircraft Inspections (AV1ATES)

Here's a scenario: you pre-flight the aircraft, everything looks great, the engine starts right up — but the logbook sitting in the back pocket shows the annual inspection expired three weeks ago. You haven't left the ramp, but you're already in violation of federal aviation regulations. The airworthiness inspection system exists to prevent exactly this, and the DPE will probe every corner of it.

**AV1ATES — the seven inspection categories.** Every aircraft operating under Part 91 must comply with this inspection stack. Think of it as layered maintenance accountability:

- **A — Annual Inspection.** Every 12 calendar months. Required for *all* civil aircraft. Must be performed by an A&P mechanic holding an **Inspection Authorization (IA)** — a standard A&P without the IA designation can do the work but cannot sign off the return to service.
- **V — VOR Check.** Every 30 days. This one is **IFR-only** — not required for VFR operations. The DPE loves this fact because most students apply it to all operations.
- **1 — 100-Hour Inspection.** Every 100 hours of flight time. Required **only** when the aircraft is used commercially: carrying passengers for hire, or provided by an instructor for flight training. A standard A&P (no IA required) can perform and sign off a 100-Hour. And here's the elegant part: a completed Annual *supersedes* the 100-Hour — it resets both clocks simultaneously.
- **A — Altimeter/Pitot-Static.** Every 24 calendar months. IFR in controlled airspace only.
- **T — Transponder.** Every 24 calendar months. Required for all operations requiring a transponder (Classes A/B/C/D and above 10,000 MSL).
- **E — ELT.** Every 12 calendar months for battery/installation check. Battery replacement trigger: 50% of useful life expired, or 1 cumulative hour of use.
- **S — Static System.** Covered under the Altimeter check above.

**The 100-Hour: the most misunderstood inspection.** The most reliable oral exam mistake is a student who thinks the 100-Hour applies to their personal flights. It does not. You can fly your own aircraft 500 hours without a 100-Hour inspection ever being required — as long as you're not charging for it. The moment you put one passenger on board for compensation, or the flight school dispatches that aircraft for student training, the clock starts.

**The Annual expiration trap.** The Annual expires at midnight on the last day of the 12th calendar month following the inspection date. There is **no grace period** for an overdue Annual — none. If your Annual expired yesterday, the aircraft is unairworthy today. It cannot fly, even 15 minutes to the maintenance shop, without a Special Flight Permit. This is different from the 100-Hour, which has a 10-hour grace window specifically for ferrying to a maintenance facility.

**The 100-Hour math that kills students on checkrides.** This calculation trips up nearly every applicant. The regulation (91.409(b)) allows up to 10 overage hours while en route to a maintenance facility — but those hours are **permanently debited** from the next interval. Fix the formula in your memory: *Next inspection due = last inspection time + (100 − overage)*. Fly 6 hours over? Next interval is only 94 hours long — not 100. The FAA doesn't give back what you borrowed.

**Recordkeeping: the four elements of 43.9.** An inspection that wasn't properly logged is legally as if it never happened. Every maintenance entry must contain: (1) a description of the work, (2) the date of completion, (3) the name of the person who performed the work, and (4) the signature, certificate number, and type of certificate held by the person approving the return to service. One missing element — especially the certificate number — and the aircraft hasn't legally been returned to airworthy condition, even if the mechanic did perfect work.

**The checkride trap:** Students know AV1ATES but apply every inspection to every flight. The VOR check and Altimeter/Pitot-Static are IFR-specific. And when the DPE asks whether a personal-use aircraft needs a 100-Hour, the answer is no — unless money is changing hands for the flight.
